analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll resume arguments in Oppenheimer Fund against Sanders. I understand you're submitting now. Chief Justice, I have been informed that only nine minutes of my time remain, and with your leave, I would like to reserve those for a rebuttal. You may do so. Thank you. Mr. Ruby, you may proceed. Mr. Chief Justice, it may please the Court. Before proceeding with the body of my argument, I would like to correct an erroneous statement that was made by Petitionist Counsel yesterday in response to a question, I believe, from Mr. Justice Rehnquist. Contrary to petitionist contention, a request for information as to the names and addresses of class members pursuant to the discovery rules was orally made by plaintiffs at a conference with the District Court in June 1974. And the defendants had a full opportunity to argue in the District Court that the cost of discovering this information should be borne by the plaintiffs rather than the defendants. This is manifestly clear from the briefs submitted by the parties in July of 1974 as requested by the District Court dealing with the issue of whether such information may be obtained through discovery, and if so, the appropriate allocation of the cost of discovering this information in this case. Mr. Ruby, what was the ruling of the District Court on that discovery motion? Mr. Justice Rehnquist, the Court finally issued a decision, as you know, in which it determined that the defendant should bear the cost of obtaining this information. As I will indicate in connection with the brief submitted, the matter of the application of the discovery rules and who should bear the cost under them was argued and considered. The District Court did not specifically, in its opinion, make reference to it. But I think the thrust of petitioners' position is that they were in some way prejudiced because they had no opportunity to, in effect, make a protective order or to deal with the question. And I think as far as that is concerned, the record would indicate clearly that they had a full opportunity to express their views. One of the District Court's reasons, as I read it, for requiring your opponents to bear the $16,000 cost was that they had opposed your motion to define the class action. And I would think that might have more relevance if it had gone on class action, so far as Judge Grazer was concerned, than if it had come up at the discovery stage. Well, I think, Mr. Justice Rehnquist, and I cannot, of course, say precisely what was in Judge Grise's mind, but I can say clearly that he did give consideration to the question of the discovery rules. For example, if I may just refer to a brief submitted by the unaffiliated defendants, which was requested by Judge Grise. And I'm quoting now from Document 90, which is referred to in the Index of Documents Filed in the Appendix. Page 3 of the defendant's brief says, Since the discovery here sought is solely for the purpose of enabling plaintiffs to fulfill their obligations under Rule 23, the cost of such discovery should clearly be borne by plaintiffs. They go on on page 4 to say, Even if, as suggested by the court, meaning the district court, the cost of identifying the members of the class to whom notice can be mailed is a cost of discovery, the pertinent decisions in the area of discovery make it clear that such costs must be borne by the plaintiffs. And likewise, the defendant Oppenheimer Manager Corporation submitted a brief in which one of their topic headings was in Document 92. Under the discovery rules, the cost of identifying class members are properly chargeable to the plaintiffs. So at least I think it's clear that the court considered it and they had a full opportunity to argue it. But you said Judge Grise did not rule on it. Well, I cannot say that, Mr. Chief Justice. I can simply say he didn't specifically refer to it in his opinion, but I think a fair reading of his opinion would indicate that he considered all of the arguments that were made. Mr. Ruby. Yes. Judge Mulligan, in his opinion, said that the plaintiffs have never sought discovery relief under Rule 34. I take it you view that as erroneous. Mr. Justice Powell, I view that as erroneous. It is true that we did not file a piece of paper, but I don't think that's really the issue here. At a conference with the district court, an application was made, considered, and everyone had an opportunity to address themselves to it. Orally? Orally, yes, sir. But, Mr. Ruby, that was before the class had been determined, was it not? Yes, it was, Mr. Justice. What exactly did you request orally? What we requested, Mr. Justice Stevens, was that if this information should be required. What information? That is, information as to the names and addresses of class members. Which you couldn't possibly know who they'd be until you knew what the class was, did you? Well, we had requested the class definition, Mr. Justice Stevens. We had asked the court to define a class which would encompass people between March 28, 1968, and April 24, 1970, and who were still stockholders of the fund. Now, we took the position. And, of course, your opponents took a different view of what the process was. They opposed. They opposed our class definition. And the court agreed with them. The court issued a decision, Mr. Justice Stevens, in which it determined that it would accept the proposal made by the defendants. But I would respectfully submit that a fair reading of the district court's opinion, and the whole proceedings relating there, too, would indicate that the district court was issuing a decision which really was interrelated in the sense that it was considering what the various proposals were. And I think it took into account the defendant's position as to the class definition and then determined that, and I don't think it determined necessarily on this ground alone, but at least it took into account that fact in deciding that it should have the defendant's fair decision. But if I understand you correctly, if he had granted your discovery request at the time you'd made it, namely asking for those who were still stockholders in 1970, you still would have needed more. No, Mr. Justice. Because that wouldn't have been the whole class. Mr. Justice Stevens, if I can answer you in this way. Our position was that if we had the class defined as we had proposed, which was the people who bought during this period but were still stockholders of the fund, it would not have been necessary at all to obtain this information because what we could have done is to send out a notice to all the current stockholders of the fund, directing, of course, the notice, in a sense, having an introductory part that said this is directed to those who purchased during this period. If we had done that, individual notice would have gone to all the class members. The class would have been sufficiently defined so the judgment could have been entered under the rules of 23C3, and the information would not have been needed at all. So what we were really saying to the district court is, Your Honor, we don't think we need this information. However, if you were to accept the position taken, then we ask that it be obtained through this government. The main issue before this court, at least as initially presented by petitioners' brief, is whether the district court had discretion to require defendant Oppenheimer fund to bear the expense of identifying class members in this case, as the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit held in its en banc decision, or whether, as the petitioners contend, there should be a hard and fast rule in all cases that the plaintiff must bear the expense of obtaining information as to the names and addresses of class members, and that the district court should have no discretion in this area. It would appear from petitioners' argument yesterday, during which petitioner scarcely mentioned this question, that petitioner does not place great weight upon its position on this issue. The petitioner instead appeared to place primary emphasis upon a subsidiary contention, that is, that the district court abused its discretion by requiring the defendant fund to bear the expense of culling out the names of class members from its computer tapes, and that the court of appeals erred in affirming the district court's discretionary determination. The question of whether the district court abused its discretion is a rather limited one, since, of course, the issue is not what appellate judges would have done in like circumstances, but rather was the district court's determination so clearly erroneous or arbitrary as to constitute an abuse of discretion. I might note that this court, in fact, has usually declined to even review cases involving discretionary determinations. In the instant case, as I will more fully discuss in my argument later, the district court's discretionary determination was well supported by the record in this case, by the applicable discovery rule, and by well-recognized commentators on the subject. You're relying then on the discovery provisions? We say, Mr. Justice Rehnquist, that the district court had discretion in this case, and we believe that the discovery rules are applicable. Well, if it weren't the discovery rules, what statutory or case authority is there for the district court to shift the cost of financing a part of the lawsuit from the plaintiff to the defendant? Well, of course, without in any way wanting to give the impression that we do not have firm reliance on the discovery rules, I would only suggest this to you, Mr. Justice Rehnquist. In the Nissen case, which my adversary relies upon heavily, the court took the position that it did not believe that the discovery rules controlled or governed the question of whether or not the plaintiff or the defendant should obtain the information and who should pay for it. Although it did say that the spirit of those rules and the decisional law under them may offer guidance. It felt, however, that Rule 23D was, in fact, the more appropriate rule. But I think the important thing from Nissen is that the court in that case, the Fifth Circuit, reviewed the decisions in this area and noted that the courts, contrary to what this court had indicated in Isen, that is that the cost of preparing and mailing a notice has to, under the usual rule, be borne by the plaintiff, the courts that have dealt with the question of the identification of class members or the obtaining of information there, too, had in some cases placed the burden on the plaintiffs, in some cases placed the burden on the defendants, because it was recognized there that you were not dealing with the same kind of activity and that the district courts should have discretion. And even the Fifth Circuit, Mr. Justice Rehnquist, did not set down any hard and fast rule. Do you think the district court would have authority if the plaintiff came in and made a motion saying that he had run out of fees to pay his attorney and needed $10,000 to continue to maintain the lawsuit to require the defendant to supply the plaintiff with $10,000 pending the outcome of the lawsuit? Not at all, sir. Not at all, sir. But I think this is an entirely different situation. What happens if he comes in and says, I have ordered these records and they cost $17,000, I only have seven? I would say this, Mr. Justice Marshall, that the question would not be whether or not the plaintiff has the money. And we don't take the position that this determination is based on... But you do recognize that back in the good old days, the defendant would tell you to go shop, wouldn't he? Yes, he would, sir. Yes, he would. And I'm not arguing to this court... So aren't you stuck with the discovery rule? I would say certainly that is our primary position. I simply wanted to point out, in response to Mr. Justice Rehnquist's question, that even the Fifth Circuit and Nissen, which the defendants rely on heavily, recognized that there should be discretion in this area, even if Rule 23D were to be appropriate rather than discovery rules. Since the petition is due to vote a fairly extensive... Mr. Ruby, on the question of discretion, do you think that it was an appropriate exercise of discretion for the trial judge to rely on the fact that since the defendants had taken a position with respect to the proper definition of the class and he agreed with them, that therefore they should pay the cost? I think it was fair, Mr. Justice Stevens. I think, as the Court of Appeals pointed out, the arguments made by the defendants may have been entitled to some consideration, but they did not require a determination that the class should be defined as the defendants wanted to have it defined. I think this Court has indicated that classes may be defined in various ways. There is no magical one definition necessarily, and I think in a footnote in the Eisen case, this Court indicated that it may be permissible for the plaintiff in that case to redefine his class with the specific intention of reducing the costs of notice involved. I would say this in answer to your question, Mr. Justice Stevens, that if a defendant takes a position and says, I want to have a class defined more broadly than the plaintiff does, I think it's fair for a Court, as long as you're not dealing with an obviously improper class that the plaintiff was proposing, and I suggest we did not offer it in proper class, and I think the Court of Appeals believe that to be the case. But your class would have excluded people who had, in some kind of an equitable sense, an equal interest in the recovery. Not necessarily, Mr. Justice Stevens. They would have paid too much for their shares, wouldn't they? No, I think there is a distinction which even the Court of Appeals noted, that people who were no longer stockholders because they had both bought and sold might not have been damaged because they might have been selling during the period. So I would suggest that it was a fair point for the district court to take into account. What is your reason for saying that notice and the names of parties should be treated differently? Well, if I may get to that, Mr. Justice White. Before you do, let me ask you this. You say this is a discretionary power of the district court. Now, what factors would enter that discretion? Assume hypothetically a case where instead of $16,000 as it is now, or it was at the time the case arose, the cost was $100,000. Would the judge be able to say as part of his exercise of discretion, well, that's just too much. We won't go that high. Is the cost one factor? What enters into the exercise of discretion? Mr. Chief Justice, I think that the question here is not dissimilar from the problem which faces a district court any time it is dealing with discovery questions. If a plaintiff seeks to obtain information from a defendant or the other way around, the question of whether or not the burden involved is undue, and I think that is the critical thing, whether it is undue, is a factor which the district court must consider. And if we sought to require a defendant or in another case, another litigant sought to require his adversary to produce information that cost him $100,000, as you've indicated, Mr. Chief Justice, it's quite possible the district court would say that's an undue burden and would enter some order which would protect the interests of the defendant. So I think that what you're dealing with here is the facts in this case, and I suggest to the court that based upon the facts in this case, it cannot be said that the district court abused its discretion. If I might go on, and I think in answering Mr. Justice White... Do you think the court would have it within its power, its discretionary power, requirement that the plaintiff split up a bond and it was sufficient to cover the costs? Yes, yes. He could have done that here, you think? He was asked to do so. He was asked to do so. But I think he considered the fact that bonds, of course, are onerous. Was it really necessary? I think the petitioner indicated in response to a question from Mr. Justice Brennan yesterday that the plaintiffs here had about $25,000 worth of stock. I don't think the district court felt under the circumstances it was necessary. The defendant's argument on this point about the question of a hard and fast rule is based upon the premise that the plaintiff is required in all cases to bear the cost of discovering or obtaining information as to the names and addresses of class members under Eisen 4 as part of his obligation to bear the cost of printing and mailing the notice to the class. Eisen 4, however, did not hold, as defendants erroneously claim, that information as to the names and addresses of class members may not be obtained through discovery, nor did it indicate that the cost of obtaining this information must be borne in all cases by the plaintiff. In point of fact, Eisen 4 did not even deal with the question of allocating the cost of obtaining information as to the names of class members. Defendants argue, nevertheless, that it is a prerequisite to sending the notice mandated by Eisen 4 that plaintiffs obtain the names and addresses of those to whom the notice will be sent, and therefore, the cost of obtaining this information must be borne by the plaintiff under Eisen 4. Defendants' argument is not well founded for several reasons. First, defendants mistakenly assume that simply because it is necessary to obtain the names and addresses of class members prior to giving notice to the class, this information may not be obtained under the discovery rules. If this were true, however, it would also logically follow that information relating to the definition or scope of the class, whether the members of the class can be identified through reasonable effort, what is the best practicable notice under the circumstances, all of which presumably must be obtained prior to giving notice to the class could not be obtained through discovery. Yet in this very case, discovery was permitted by the district court without objection by the defendants with respect to these matters and other matters relating to the method and cost of sending notice to the class. And indeed, defendants in their reply brief, I believe on page 9, appear to concede the fact that such information may be obtained through discovery. If plaintiffs are permitted under the discovery rules to obtain information as to all of these matters pertaining to class action requirements, it would be arbitrary, we submit, to hold that the plaintiffs may not obtain information under the discovery rules as to the names and addresses of the class members. So it looks like to know it's a cost. Well, I think, Mr. Justice White, that basically what I'm saying is that if you are talking about the discovery rules, that the question of the allocation of costs becomes a matter within the discretion of the district court and the question is normally whether there is an undue burden or expense. Yes, maybe so, but the argument on the other side, I would imagine, and I think it is, that the discretion is controlled by Rule 23 policies with respect to costs. Well, I think there is no authority, Mr. Justice White, that would suggest that the discovery rules and the policies under the discovery rules should not apply. Even the Nissen case, as I mentioned before, which is the only court I know of which has really suggested that Rule 23D rather than discovery rules might be governing the issue. Even Nissen says that the discovery rules, the spirit of those rules, the decisional law under them may provide guidance with regard to the question of the allocation of costs. So that I would really suggest to the court that while we believe that the discovery rules are applicable as the Court of Appeals in its unbanked decision found and we've cited authority in our brief supporting that decision and I think the federal discovery rules themselves, the language of it supports our position. But even if you were to say, as the Nissen Court did, that Rule 23D should govern, I think it's a distinction without a difference because I think the issue is still whether or not within the discretion of the court there is an undue burden or expense and that the spirit of the discovery rules would apply anyway. Why wouldn't Rule 33C govern if it's the discovery rules where it says the burden of deriving or ascertaining the answer is substantially the same for the party serving and the interrogatory is for the party served? Well, the Court of Appeals dealt with that, Mr. Justice McQuiston. I'd like to answer your question. Do you rely on anything other than Judge Hayes' distinction? Well, we rely on, first of all, the fact that what we're dealing with here is clearly computerized information. We're dealing with computer tapes. We're dealing with computer material. But isn't it a fact that the defendant would have had to prepare a new program in order to provide you with this information? It isn't as if he could just have a printout on an existing computer system. That is true, Mr. Justice Rehnquist. But in terms of what is the appropriate rule, as you've asked, I think the rules themselves, plus the textual commentators, I think have recognized, also the advisory committee notes have recognized, that there is a significant difference in how you treat discovery of ordinary business records and how you treat discovery of computerized information. Of course, in the Second Circuit's unbanked opinion, they pointed out that Rule 34 is specifically applicable to the computerized information. And in the opinion, the court indicated that unlike Rule 34, Rule 33 was not especially tailored to the discovery problems posed by contemporary computer technology. And then the court also went on to say that the draftsman of Rule 34 chose wisely, in light of the relative judicial inexperience with discovery problems posed by computer technology, not to burden discovery of computerized information with the more rigid principle of Rule 33C. Well, what difference does it really make what the process is? If it costs $16,000, what difference does it make whether it has to be done manually or by a computer or by some other method? I think it makes this difference, Mr. Chief Justice. The concept behind Rule 33C is that there are records, ordinary business records, and that one party, the responding party, can simply take these records and turn them over to the discovering party because the burden of going through the records and examining them is the same for both parties. But we're not dealing with that situation here. It is unrealistic to say that we can take their computer tapes, we can take their computerized information as we would take ordinary business records. Is it true that they don't have that on computer? Mr. Justice Marshall, is that true or false? They have the information on the computer tapes, but it is necessary for them to add to existing programs in order to extract the information from the computer tapes. I thought in 58 or whatever it was, 58 and 59? 68 and 69. Those are not on computer tapes at all. No, sir. I think it's clear from the record in this case and all the decisions that what we're dealing with here is information on computer tapes, but it's quite true that it is necessary to add to existing programs. Now, we're not just dealing with some records or some papers. We're dealing with tapes and information on tapes. Don't you think that when the rule was adopted, they were talking about where it existed, was already programmed, and all you had to do was push a couple of buttons. Isn't that what they were talking about? I don't think so, Mr. Justice Marshall. Well, let me quote from Professors Wright and Miller's treatise, which I think has been fairly well accepted in dealing with these matters. Anything from Moore? I think that, no, but if I may, I'll just at least quote from the Wright and Miller. I don't think Moore dealt with it in the same way that Wright and Miller did. Wright and Miller say, the responding party who is required to prepare a printout or otherwise make the data reasonably usable for the discovering party must ordinarily bear the expense of doing this. He can shift the cost to the discovering party only on a showing under Rule 26C that Justice so requires in order to protect himself from undue burden or expense. In many instances, the peculiarities of computerized information actually will oblige the disclosing party to engage in fairly sophisticated electronic manipulation and analysis of the data in his computer system. Mr. Ruby? Yes, sir. Who has this information? The information is in the possession of the defendant's transfer agent. The transfer agent? Yes, sir. The transfer agent is not a party to this case, is it? The transfer agent is not a party to this case, but has been essentially treated and I think the parties have treated this as the defendant's agent. Is that conceded? The defendants have not raised such a question, Mr. Justice Powell. I'm sure that the defendants pay the transfer agent, but to whom does the transfer agent owe its primary duty? I think the defendant. To the defendant? I think to the defendant. What about the holders of the shares? It would be my understanding, sir, that they are employed by and retained by the fund, by the defendant's fund. Let's assume for the moment that the material you seek were in the hands of a wholly independent party. How would you proceed to get it? I think if the information I was seeking were not in the hands of the defendant, and I have treated, and they have treated it as, in effect, being in their hands, you have a wholly different case, because we're proceeding on the basis that we are seeking, in effect, through discovery. You agree, do you, that if the information were in the hands of an independent party, you have to subpoena that and pay any costs that were involved? I think there would be entirely different issues involved, even where you're dealing with third parties, Mr. Justice Powell, and you can seek under the federal rules discovery from them, but the district court would then have to make a decision in the context of the fact that you're seeking it from a third party having no relationship to either the plaintiff or the defendant. So I would only say you'd have a different issue, and I would only conclude by saying here that we are in a situation here where we have a very different situation than you have where you have ordinary business records. I see that my time is up, and I will only conclude by saying that we believe that the Court of Appeals was correct in holding that there was discretion under the discovery rules and that the district court did not abuse its discretion. And for all of those... Just before you sit down, because I didn't quite finish before, what factor is there that supports the exercise of the discretion the way the district judge exercises? Just the fact there's a lot of money in the fund? No, sir. No, sir. I think what would support their position is the Court of Appeals in reviewing this pointed out two things. They said, first of all, that the burden... Defend and oppose the class, and there's a relatively small amount of money involved. Well, not a relatively small amount. They said that the burden imposed was not unreasonable in light of the nature of the information sought and the extent and character of the fund's business operations. The Court of Appeals pointed out that there was not an injustice, when you're talking about whether it's an undue burden or expense, there was not an injustice in requiring one whose business is vast and complex to go to proportionally greater lengths, and they also pointed out that it was not unreasonable to demand of a respondent that it employ its computer resources to provide discoverable information of a relatively simple nature, whereas, in this case, the respondent fund makes extensive use of computers in the operation of its business. So really, what they were doing is considering whether the burden was undue, and for those reasons, plus the fact that they said it wasn't unreasonable because the defendant had, in effect, necessitated the cost by opposing the class definition. So it was a combination of those things, and I would support that, given the rather limited consideration here about abuse of discretion, that it should not be found that the Court abused its discretion. So I would respectfully submit that the Court of Appeals' unbanked decision should be the transfer agent, assuming the defendants had authorized the transfer agent to give you the information. By the information, Mr. Justice White, do you mean give us the raw material? No, no. I mean, whatever it was you wanted the defendants to furnish you with, they were going to get it from the transfer agent, I take it. Yes, sir. And they're the ones who had the information. Yes, sir. Now, if they had said to the transfer agent to furnish it to the plaintiffs, but get the money, get the cost from them, would it have cost you approximately the same amount of money as it would have cost the defendants, $16,000? I can't answer your question other than saying that I have no information that it would cost us more or less. It's possible that because of their relationship with the defendant, it might cost the defendant less, but I really think that. Assuming it would cost you the identical amount of money, you still think it's a Rule 34 thing rather than a 33 matter? I would say, yes, yes, sir. I would say that the federal rules and the text writers, and I think that it is a Rule 34 case. Thank you. On the question of what the district court had before it and what, in the way of a request for discovery, the district court's opinion at the very outset states that plaintiffs have moved for class action treatment of a part of these consolidated cases, which consists of both class and derivative claims, certain problems have been raised mainly as to the definition of the class and as to who is to bear certain expenses connected with the giving of notice. That is the issue that the defendant, that the district court thought he was dealing with. He didn't say we have here a problem in relation to the discovery rule, but as who is to bear the cost of giving notice. Now, Mr. Ruby says that giving notice doesn't necessarily mean coming up with a list of names and addresses to which the notices are to be sent. But if you're going to start to fragment the giving of notice, then he might as well say, Eisenfore, in saying that it's the duty of the plaintiffs to pay for the cost of notice, doesn't say that we have to pay for the cost of printing the letters to go to the security holders. But the defendants, they may even have a printing press in their plant. Let them print the notices. It merely says that we have to pay the cost of sending the notices once you start to fragment what is involved here. Mr. Berman, could I interrupt because it's one, the district judge seemed to place great emphasis on the fact that the defendant's position with respect to the definition of the class was adopted. And since the defendants urged a particular definition, they should be responsible. And it's kind of a strange situation. If I understand it correctly, the defendants wanted a larger class than the plaintiffs did. Is that correct? No. There was a shifting about in this sense during the course of the proceedings in district court. The plaintiffs, of course, initially asked that the class must be defined precisely as it was finally defined in the court's order. That is covering that two-year period. I understood him to say that he asked for to exclude those who had sold their shares. After the decision in Eisen III came down and it became clear that the plaintiffs would have to bear the cost of notice if Eisen III were sustained by this court, then the plaintiffs tried to diminish the cost and they said, well, let's drop out all those shareholders who are no longer shareholders. Now, why did the defendants oppose that? And the defendants opposed it because as they read the, as they read Eisen IV, Eisen IV said it is an unambiguous requirement of Rule 23 that members of the class receive no individual notice. And it seemed to them very... Well, that's after the class has been defined. But I'm asking, why did the defendant... It's normally in the defendant's interest to have a smaller class because their liability, potential liability is thereby smaller. In fact, the defendant... Why did they oppose a smaller definition of the class in this case? Because we felt, as the district judge concluded, that this was an arbitrary and unreasonable exclusion of those who were properly in the class. And if we proceeded on that basis... Could the district court have reasonably inferred that you thought this might impose an additional notice cost on the plaintiffs and therefore possibly win the lawsuit? Well, I can't see how he could in view of his saying that this is an arbitrary reduction of the class and I will not do it. The defendants were really trying to protect the benefits of these fringe members of the plaintiff's class and protect the interests of those members of the class who would be excluded by... Narrowing the definition. ...it seemed to us that the district judge, having concluded that it would be an arbitrary exclusion that he couldn't sustain, then to turn around and say to us that now you pay for it because you raised the question with which I've reached agreement and therefore you pay for it for... It's just a sort of an interest in symmetry. It would have been arbitrary to exclude him. That's the only reason. There was no financial gain for the defendants by narrowing the class. No, not a...
